claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is primarily controlled by electronic factors, specifically valence electron concentration (VEC).
VEC governs local chemical bonding and lattice distortion in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys.
Reducing Al content while holding the ratios of the other elements constant increases VEC.
A slight reduction in Al favors a stable single FCC phase over a mixed-phase microstructure.
The higher-Al baseline alloy typically has a mixed-phase microstructure.
The baseline mixed microstructure includes brittle BCC or intermetallic phases.
VEC directly influences local chemical order and lattice distortion.
VEC-induced changes in local chemical order and lattice distortion mediate selection of a uniform FCC structure when Al is reduced.
Increasing VEC by reducing Al strengthens metallic bonds that favor the FCC arrangement.
Reducing Al suppresses formation of secondary BCC or ordered phases.
Suppressing secondary phases retards phase transformation and microstructural degradation under thermal, radiation, and cryogenic stresses.
The reduced-Al alloy will predominantly exhibit a stable single-phase FCC structure with fewer secondary precipitates than the baseline.
The reduced-Al alloy will have improved high-temperature strength relative to the baseline.
The reduced-Al alloy will have better radiation tolerance relative to the baseline.
The reduced-Al alloy will have enhanced cryogenic toughness relative to the baseline.
An FCC-favoring reduction in Al helps retain environmental resistance.
The proposed relationship applies to conventionally processed bulk Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys under the specified thermal, radiation, and mechanical environments.
The relationship may not extend to powder-metallurgy or additively manufactured material, or to compositions in which changes in other elements overcompensate the effect of Al on VEC.
